strengths: AVIS addresses a meaningful gap between audio-visual semantic segmentation and video instance tracking: distinguishing individual sounding objects and maintaining their identities as sound activity changes. AVISeg is a substantial contribution, with 94,074 masks across 926 videos averaging 61.4 seconds, including silent and simultaneous-source frames.

The baseline has convincing comparative support on established metrics. Under the reported common ResNet-50 initialization and training schedule, AVISM achieves 61.73 HOTA and 40.57 mAP, exceeding VITA's 57.48/36.25 and audio-aware COMBO's 57.39/37.84 (Table 2). Thus, its advantage does not depend solely on the proposed FSLA metric.

The architecture sensibly combines frame-level sound localization with temporal association through compact object tokens. Table 4 shows successive improvements from frame-level and video-level audio fusion, while Table 7 supports the similarity loss. Backbone and window-size experiments provide additional characterization.

The manuscript clearly illustrates the task and architecture, and the supplement supplies useful optimization details, baseline prompts, qualitative comparisons, and candid failure cases. The stated dataset/code release increases its potential usefulness. The benchmark contribution and corroborating standard-metric gains support weak acceptance.
weaknesses: FSLA has a substantive specification problem. Algorithm 1 increments the silent-frame success counter without checking that predictions are empty, initializes counters outside the IoU-threshold loop, and omits explicit checks for equal instance counts and correctness of every matched instance. Class averaging is also unclear. These discrepancies prevent faithful reproduction from the manuscript, although they do not establish that the reported implementation is wrong. The assertion that mAP never penalizes non-sounding predictions is also too broad: false positives can reduce precision.

Annotation reliability is insufficiently documented for the benchmark's hardest requirement. Section 4 describes SAM-assisted masks and repeated manual refinement, but gives no quantitative quality audit or procedure for resolving ambiguous sound attribution among similar instances. It also leaves unclear how sound activity within a one-second clip determines the label at the sampled frame. Mask quality and correct sounding-instance attribution are distinct concerns.

The broad conclusions about multimodal large models exceed the evaluation evidence. Supplement E explicitly merges same-category masks into one identity for Sam4AVS and BuboGPT, and treats each category as one instance for AL-Ref-SAM 2; Sam4AVS additionally receives only the top-ranked audio class. These adapters constrain the very instance discrimination being evaluated. Table 3 establishes limitations of these particular pipelines, but cannot isolate limitations of the underlying models.

The central challenge of multiple sounding instances from the same category is not evaluated separately. FSLAm combines different-category and same-category mixtures, while Figure 10 identifies same-category ambiguity as a prominent failure mode. With 539 videos involving music and evaluation at 1 FPS, aggregate results provide limited evidence about broader scene diversity or precise sound onset/offset tracking.

Methodological originality is modest because object-token association and shifted-window processing largely follow VITA and established Transformer designs. The claimed computational and long-range advantages are only partially established: Table 5 reports maximum frame capacity versus window size, but lacks matched runtime/memory comparisons and performance stratified by video length or reappearance gap. This limits the model-specific contribution more than the benchmark's value.
